title: Speech online
hookLine: the same rules apply to messages and posts
tomorrow: tara starts it again at lunch. what if simran says nothing?

lines: A CANDLE, A CAPTION, A JAB.
DEATH AND LIFE, IN THE TONGUE.
cards: It's a good post. Simran has rewritten it four times: funny, cutting, nothing anyone could report. A photo of a candle, captioned: some of us are actually nice in real life.

She and Maya are studying at Maya's grandma's kitchen table. Maya's grandma reads the screen over her glasses and quotes the Bible she keeps by the stove: Death and life are in the power of the tongue.
Then she adds, and the thumbs too, these days.

teach.h: DOES A POST COUNT AS SPEECH?
teach.b: So, the question: does a post count as speech? Sikh teaching answers in Sheikh Farid's voice, in saloks kept in the Guru Granth Sahib.
In paraphrase: don't speak even one harsh word, because the true Master lives in everyone.

teach.h: FARID: EVERY HEART IS A JEWEL.
teach.b: Don't break anyone's heart; every heart is a priceless jewel. There's no exception for screens. A reply under someone's photo lands in the same heart a spoken word would.
The screen just lets you skip seeing their face.

teach.h: PROVERBS: DEATH AND LIFE, THE TONGUE.
teach.b: Maya's grandma was quoting Proverbs, in the King James Bible: Death and life are in the power of the tongue: and they that love it shall eat the fruit thereof.
Two traditions, and something they share: words are never small. They build or they break, and they come back to the one who speaks.
And one honest difference. Proverbs weighs speech by its fruit, what it grows in the speaker's own life. Farid weighs it by who is listening: a heart with the Master living in it.
Two angles on the same tongue, neither one cancelling the other.
Here's the line to tell a friend tonight: there's no one at the other end of a post who isn't a jewel. Simran deletes the candle. Then she sends Kiran a chemistry meme instead.

how: Some Sikh teachers apply Farid's saloks on harsh words to messages and posts: the same heart receives them, so the same care applies.

o: posting only upbeat things about your life
treating posts and messages as real speech
keeping your accounts private so you stay safe

p: every heart is a priceless jewel
death and life, in the tongue
the fruit in the speaker's life
the heart of the one listening

s: what you type counts less than what you say out loud
Farid's line has no exception for screens: every heart is a jewel.
Proverbs says death and life are in the power of the tongue
in the King James Bible, Proverbs 18:21.
Farid and Proverbs say exactly the same thing
they share that words build or break; Proverbs weighs the fruit, Farid the listener's heart.

games.q: a classmate posts a shaky cover of a song, and the comments are brutal. you have a funny line ready. what fits Farid's saloks?
o: skip the line; if you comment, say one true, kind thing.
post it; jokes online land softer than ones said aloud.
post it on a fake account, so it can't hurt your name.
games.why: the same heart reads a comment that would hear a spoken word. every heart is a jewel, so the same care applies online.

practice: Hold your phone with the screen dark, and just look at it: a small thing that carries your words into a lot of hearts. Bring to mind one person whose message you could answer kindly, and the few words you'd use.
Then set it face down and rest your hands for the sit.

wordCard.voice: Speech online. Posts, comments and replies: speech with the face hidden, landing in the same heart. Maanak means a jewel.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: maanak, a jewel; Farid's word for every heart.

carryVoice: Kind online: every reader at the other end of a post is somebody's jewel. Catch you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Ang 1384 (Salok Farid: ik phikka na gaalaae, sabhna mai sacha dhani; hiaao na kaihee thaahi, maanak sabh amolvay), paraphrased
